meta.title: Brutally Honest Ratings of VIETNAM - ft. Hanoi- Train street, Trang An Boat Tour and more
meta.description:
Welcome to Part 1 of our Vietnam travel series, where we give you brutally honest ratings on everything — from the places we stay at to the tourist spots we hit. We also share some useful information about Vietnam that might help you with your travel plans. No filters. No sugarcoating. Just real travel stories and genuine reactions, to answer the question - Should you travel to Vietnam?

In this episode, we explore Hanoi, decode popular tourist myths, reveal hidden gems, and break down exactly what you should know before travelling to Vietnam.

If you like this video, you can't imagine what PART 2 looks like! SO ⬇️

🔔 Subscribe to join us on this wild journey: https://www.youtube.com/@RohitandKanu

💬 Drop your questions in the comments, and let us know which Travel Destinations you'd like us to visit next!

FOLLOW US ON INSTAGRAM!
Rohit's IG: https://www.instagram.com/rohitsukheja/
Kanupriya's IG: https://www.instagram.com/kanupriya1707/

comments.author: @samyak123456789
comments.text:
Thanks for sharing this. We are about to visit Vietnam, and I have always been interested in history, especially Ho Chi Minh, Vietnam’s struggle for independence, and the suffering its people went through during different periods of foreign occupation and war.

I am glad you also showed the darker side of that history by visiting the prison. These places are painful, but they are important because they show what people endured and how those experiences shaped a nation.

Every country has dark chapters. Colonial powers often came in the name of trade, administration or religion, but in many places local people lost their land, freedom and lives. Today, many countries openly preserve those stories through museums, prisons and memorials.

India has equally painful stories. The Cellular Jail in the Andaman Islands is only one example, where prisoners suffered brutal punishment, isolation, forced labour and terrible conditions. There are also accounts of prisoners being left in remote and dangerous places with almost no chance of survival. These stories deserve to be preserved and told openly.

What I find difficult to understand is that when India strongly talks about its own colonial suffering, it is sometimes quickly labelled as propaganda or nationalism.

Remembering history does not mean hating people today, and it does not mean rejecting Western culture. There is nothing wrong with learning from the West or appreciating its culture. The problem is when we follow it so blindly that we become uncomfortable talking about what colonial powers once did to our own people.

I saw something similar in Korea, where museums and preserved villages openly show the suffering people faced during the Japanese occupation. Vietnam does the same. Many countries do. So why should India feel uncomfortable doing the same?

We can respect people today while still being honest about history. Preserving painful history is not hatred or propaganda. It is about respecting those who suffered and making sure future generations understand what happened. That is the hypocrisy I struggle to understand.

The question I often ask is: *why are we comfortable learning about the darkest chapters of other countries, but sometimes uncomfortable talking openly about our own?*
